title: learning-sprint-reflections-compact-daybook
content:
Sprint intent: rapid distillation of papers + one small bench to decide next quarter spike. Mostly 2 days of reading, 1 day of sketch experiments, notes to self and a short checklist for Marco/Lina to pick up.

Top-level takeaways (high-level):
- Temporal-aware retrieval looks promising for multi-turn products: weight recency but avoid short-term overfitting. Implementation: sliding-window + decay + learned recency scorer. Paper: "Temporal Retrieval for Conversational RAG" (sketchy name) — key idea: context timestamp embeddings + learned decay multiplier.
- Token-aware batching: adapt batch composition by token-cost (not just request count). If long-tail outliers cause tail latency, cap their concurrency and route them to reserved workers or async path.
- Micro-evals matter: small, focused evals with adversarial prompts find regressions faster than large held-out suites. Keep 50 golden adv prompts per intent.
- Energy and carbon per token: SysEnergy'26 poster measured delta from quantization vs batching; batching helps energy but hurts P95 latency if not tuned. Need to measure tradeoff at our scale.

Quick paper synopses (bullet cast):
1) Temporal Retrieval for Conversational RAG — notes:
 - Setup: stream of documents, queries anchored with timestamps.
 - Model uses dual-encoder + time-aware weighting.
 - Results show better recall for recent facts, small hit on older recall.
 - Takeaway: for user-facing chat features with recency requirements, build a lightweight recency filter first (fast) then apply full retrieval.
 - Open question: how to integrate with existing prefix/KV cache so we don't double-count recency effects?

2) Token-Aware Dynamic Batching (conference poster):
 - Idea: treat token budget as resource, not request count. Use short requests to fill leftover slots in a batch.
 - Implementation complexity: per-worker queueing + admission control.
 - Measured improvement: ~8-12% throughput on mixed workloads, reduced P99 by ~10ms when tuned.
 - Implementation note: can probably prototyping using our worker-side admission hooks. Mark as experimental.

3) Calibration and Temperature Scheduling for Generation Scores (ArXiv short):
 - Why: model confidence correlates poorly with actual correctness/hallucination.
 - Approach: post-hoc temperature scaling on logits + small calibration set per-domain.
 - Impact: better reranker performance and selective-answer abstention.
 - To try: couple with our reranking pipeline for high-value flows (billing docs, legal summaries).

4) Micro-evals for Hallucination (lab notes + code repo):
 - Design: create focused adversarial probes for known failure modes (dates, counts, entity mixing).
 - Tooling: store probes as JSONL with expected structured answer; run nightly.
 - We should add 3 probes for our legal assistant persona (case citations, statute dates, jurisdiction).

Conference takeaways (ML Systems Summit, May 2027):
- Panel on "Serving Under Unpredictable Demand": people are moving toward hybrid routing (fast-path small models + async large-model fallbacks). Practical notes: metricize user-perceived P95 not server P95.
- Talk on "Kernel Selection at Scale": auto-select kernels based on quantization and attention pattern; reminded me we still have one-off kernels for a couple layers in our forks — tech debt to track.
- Poster: "Lifecycle of a Prompt": treat prompt templates as deployable artifacts with versions + evals. Good alignment with Optimize product thinking.

Experiments to run (small, actionable):
- A) Temporal-retrieval smoke test: synthetic time-shifted docset + 2 retrieval strategies (decay vs recency filter) — metric: recent-recall / stale-recall ratio. Owner: Marco. Est: 2d.
- B) Token-aware batching prototype on a single pool: instrument admission, simulate 60/30/10 mix of short/med/long. Metric: throughput, P95, energy-per-token (approx). Owner: Carmen. Est: 3d.
- C) Micro-eval harness: add 50 adversarial probes for legal assistant; add to nightly. Owner: Lina. Est: 1d + ingest.

Checklist for picking up work:
- [ ] Add ticket in GH: rag-experiments repo for Temporal retrieval (link above).
- [ ] Create dataset: synthetic time-labeled docs (script in rag-experiments/data).
- [ ] Wire up worker admission hook for token-aware batching (branch: token-batching-exper).
- [ ] Draft micro-eval JSONL format and add CI runner.
- [ ] Quick doc: pros/cons + ops runbook for enabling token-aware batching in Dedicated pools.

Notes to self (untidy):
- Watch out: combining recency weighting with prefix cache can amplify recent tokens twice — need instrumentation on end-to-end freshness weight.
- If token-aware batching reduces cost, pitch to Optimize team for an autosuggestion: "Enable token-aware batching for mixed workloads" (but show latency tradeoffs).
- For calibration: small domain-specific calibration sets (~200 examples) may be enough. We should avoid large sample costs.

Links / crumbs to follow up:
- Marco: ask for current prefix/KV cache metrics per-request (p95 mem hits)
- Lina: share micro-eval runner from legal-sims (repo id in slack)
- Add to Confluence: short write-up with experiment plan (CONFLUENCE-5678 placeholder)

Unresolved questions (research):
- How much does temporal weighting help for personas with slow-evolving facts (e.g., company org charts)?
- Best way to version prompt templates (store as JSON + hash + evaluations?)
- Can temperature scaling be done cheaply per-tenant at inference time or must be precomputed per-model?

Final thought (single line): prioritize cheap instrumentation + micro-evals before large compute spikes — find the signal early.

summary: Compact daybook of readings and tactical experiments: temporal retrieval, token-aware batching, micro-evals, calibration. Actionable experiments + checklist for eng-applied-ml.
